OpenAI was supposed to cut usage limits by 50% today. Instead Tibo announced they're doubling limits for Pro 100/200/500 and Business Premium. Alex Finn's math: 4x where limits were supposed to land. 192k views.

His workflow preview: the agent on a fast setting drives CapCut on a second monitor through computer use and makes every edit, and he improves the skill as he goes.

The lesson isn't 'OpenAI cooked'. Limits move both ways, overnight. Know what each workflow costs you, so a change like this is a decision and not a surprise.

hits.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg posted an 11-minute video on where SaaS is going, framed as 'SaaS is dead'. 145k views and 2.4k bookmarks, so people saved it to actually watch.

The headline is a hook. The useful question underneath: if software gets cheap to build, what are customers still paying for?

My answer for small builders: outcomes, data you've earned, and distribution. Write down which of the three you'd keep if your code were free tomorrow.

virals.angle: Your limits are someone else's decision
virals.draft_en:
OpenAI was set to cut usage limits in half today. Instead Tibo announced they're doubling them for Pro and Business Premium. Alex Finn's take: 4x where limits were supposed to land.

Good news this time. But it also shows that your daily workflow runs on a number someone else can change overnight.

Peter Steinberger's take the same day: use your own harness, not one where companies change what you can do at will.

Know what each of your agent workflows costs, and make sure at least one model swap is a config change.
virals.video_tip: 12s: a usage limit slider dragged down, then up, then a config file swapping models, caption own your harness.

virals.draft_en:
Cursor disclosed a security incident: a modified Claude Code VS Code extension in its extension marketplace, not built by Anthropic, affecting at most 5,000 users.

Your coding agent runs with your keys, your repo and your shell. An extension from the wrong publisher gets the same access.

Ten minutes today: list your editor extensions, check each publisher, remove what you don't use, and rotate keys if you installed something you can't verify.
virals.inspired_by: @cursor_ai extension incident (769k) + @amasad compromised extension (53k) and coding agents on laptops (18k)
virals.video_tip: 10s: an extensions list scrolling, one row with an unknown publisher highlighted and removed, then a key rotation screen, caption check the publisher.

virals.angle: What's left when code is free
virals.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg's 'SaaS is dead' video got 2.4k bookmarks. The same day he warned founders that a lot of ARR numbers going around are fake.

Put those together: building software is getting cheap, so the claims around it get louder.

What still holds value for a small builder: an outcome customers can measure, data you've earned, and an audience that trusts you. Charge for those, and report your numbers with the definition attached.
virals.inspired_by: @gregisenberg SaaS is dead (145k, 2.4k bookmarks) + fake ARR (59k)
virals.video_tip: 10s: code editor fading to grey, three solid blocks remaining (outcome, data, audience), caption charge for what's left.

virals.angle: Build the fix for your own daily annoyance
virals.draft_en:
Tony Dinh got tired of switching keyboard languages 300 times a day, so he built Vikey: it switches between English and Vietnamese as you type, 99.73% accurate by his count, free and open source. 325 bookmarks.

Same day, Pieter Levels shipped a one-line widget so travelers can show their trips on their own blog.

Neither is a big launch. Both solve something real for people who already care.

The agent writes the code now. Your job is noticing the annoyance.
virals.video_tip: 10s: a tally counter clicking every time you switch something manually, then a tiny app making the counter stop, caption notice the annoyance.

virals.draft_en:
swyx says his app design skill is the most valuable thing he's added to any model for building real working software instead of flashy demos.

The labs ship a new model every two weeks. A skill you wrote keeps working on all of them.

Write down the rules you keep repeating to your agent (design, testing, how you name things) as one skill file. Then every new model starts out already following your rules.
virals.inspired_by: @swyx app design skill (18k, 171 bookmarks) + @tdinh_me token director (7k)
virals.video_tip: 10s: model names cycling in a dropdown while one skill file stays pinned, output staying consistent, caption your rules, any model.

virals_narrative: Window Oct 29 ~11:15 CT (after Thursday's digest) through Oct 30 ~11:15 CT. The biggest watchlist posts were off-lane: Pieter Levels' Dutch burnout and European welfare thread (342k) and its follow-ups, plus a cholesterol quote and a magnesium sleep update. They're kept on the board but not drafted. On-lane, the loudest story was OpenAI reversing a planned usage cut and doubling limits for Pro and Business Premium (5.28M on Tibo's post). Alex Finn's reaction hit 192k, and Peter Steinberger used the moment to argue for owning your harness. The most-saved builder post was Greg Isenberg's 'SaaS is dead' video (2.4k bookmarks), next to his warning about fake ARR. drafts.angle: Your limits are someone else's decision
drafts.draft_en:
OpenAI was set to cut usage limits in half today. Instead Tibo announced they're doubling them for Pro and Business Premium. Alex Finn's take: 4x where limits were supposed to land.

Good news this time. But it also shows that your daily workflow runs on a number someone else can change overnight.

Peter Steinberger's take the same day: use your own harness, not one where companies change what you can do at will.

Know what each of your agent workflows costs, and make sure at least one model swap is a config change.
drafts.video_tip: 12s: a usage limit slider dragged down, then up, then a config file swapping models, caption own your harness.

drafts.draft_en:
Cursor disclosed a security incident: a modified Claude Code VS Code extension in its extension marketplace, not built by Anthropic, affecting at most 5,000 users.

Your coding agent runs with your keys, your repo and your shell. An extension from the wrong publisher gets the same access.

Ten minutes today: list your editor extensions, check each publisher, remove what you don't use, and rotate keys if you installed something you can't verify.
drafts.inspired_by: @cursor_ai extension incident (769k) + @amasad compromised extension (53k) and coding agents on laptops (18k)
drafts.video_tip: 10s: an extensions list scrolling, one row with an unknown publisher highlighted and removed, then a key rotation screen, caption check the publisher.

drafts.angle: What's left when code is free
drafts.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg's 'SaaS is dead' video got 2.4k bookmarks. The same day he warned founders that a lot of ARR numbers going around are fake.

Put those together: building software is getting cheap, so the claims around it get louder.

What still holds value for a small builder: an outcome customers can measure, data you've earned, and an audience that trusts you. Charge for those, and report your numbers with the definition attached.
drafts.inspired_by: @gregisenberg SaaS is dead (145k, 2.4k bookmarks) + fake ARR (59k)
drafts.video_tip: 10s: code editor fading to grey, three solid blocks remaining (outcome, data, audience), caption charge for what's left.

drafts.angle: Build the fix for your own daily annoyance
drafts.draft_en:
Tony Dinh got tired of switching keyboard languages 300 times a day, so he built Vikey: it switches between English and Vietnamese as you type, 99.73% accurate by his count, free and open source. 325 bookmarks.

Same day, Pieter Levels shipped a one-line widget so travelers can show their trips on their own blog.

Neither is a big launch. Both solve something real for people who already care.

The agent writes the code now. Your job is noticing the annoyance.
drafts.video_tip: 10s: a tally counter clicking every time you switch something manually, then a tiny app making the counter stop, caption notice the annoyance.

drafts.draft_en:
swyx says his app design skill is the most valuable thing he's added to any model for building real working software instead of flashy demos.

The labs ship a new model every two weeks. A skill you wrote keeps working on all of them.

Write down the rules you keep repeating to your agent (design, testing, how you name things) as one skill file. Then every new model starts out already following your rules.
drafts.inspired_by: @swyx app design skill (18k, 171 bookmarks) + @tdinh_me token director (7k)
drafts.video_tip: 10s: model names cycling in a dropdown while one skill file stays pinned, output staying consistent, caption your rules, any model.
